lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon = SGD with momentum + a post-processing step that equalizes the singular values of each 2D update, done with 5 bf16 Newton-Schulz iterations. Memory: one buffer. Extra compute: under 1% of a typical LLM training step.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muP is not a formula that predicts the best SP learning rate for a bigger model. It changes how every layer's init and update scale with width, so a wide muP model trains differently from (and in the paper's experiments, better than) a wide SP model.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops
md: Before trusting muTransfer, run a coord check over a wide range of widths with a large learning rate. Flat curves after a few steps (apart from the output and attention logits at init) mean the parametrization is right.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: FUTEX_WAIT says "sleep only if the word still holds the value I based my decision on". That expected-value check, done atomically by the kernel, is what makes lost wake-ups impossible.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed is not a weaker form of a single consistent view. Each statement sees one snapshot, but an updating statement can also see newer versions of the rows it is about to change, so a single UPDATE or DELETE can mix two moments in time. The docs call it unsuitable for commands with complex search conditions.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
md: The repair rule is not cosmetic: it changes your score. [seqeval](https://github.com/chakki-works/seqeval) documents that for gold `B-NP I-NP O` and prediction `I-NP I-NP O`, its default mode (which mimics the conlleval Perl script) gives precision, recall and F1 of 1.00, while `mode='strict'` with `scheme=IOB2` gives 0.00. Same predictions, two different papers' worth of difference. Always say which mode you used.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Choose by the edits you must survive. Resizes, recompression and tone changes: a perceptual hash with Hamming search is cheap and exact. Crops, overlays, rotations and composites: a learned copy descriptor with nearest neighbor search. Either way, tune the threshold on labeled pairs from your own traffic.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Kaminsky 2008: poisoning a whole domain
md: Kaminsky's insight was economic: random names make every attempt immediately repeatable, and forged delegations make one success worth a whole domain. The fix multiplied the guessing space by about 64,000; only signed data (DNSSEC, next lesson) removes the guessing game entirely.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Intrusion detection, network monitoring, and where to practise
md: Detection is a pipeline: sensors (Suricata, Zeek, flow exporters) produce signals, analysts and rules turn signals into decisions, and the decision must reach someone who acts. Target had the alert; the pipeline broke at the last step.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: JA4 and JARM: fingerprints that survive shuffling, and server scans
md: JARM sends traffic to the server you fingerprint. Scan only servers you own or are authorised to test, or use data from internet scanning services that already publish JARM values. Passive fingerprints (JA3, JA4, JA4S) need nothing but your own sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Layers: the OSI and TCP/IP models, and why both exist
md: Models are maps, not territory. Real protocols do not always fit one layer: ARP (lesson 5) sits between layers 2 and 3, and TLS (Transport Layer Security, the encryption under HTTPS; lesson 12) between 4 and 7. Use the numbers to communicate, not to argue about where a protocol "really" belongs.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Proxies, VPNs and firewalls
md: A VPN is not anonymity and a firewall is not a security boundary for everything. The VPN provider sees what your ISP used to see, and a firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Each control answers one question; know which one.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Simplified model: it ignores caches, assumes perfect overlap, symmetric links and that threads can saturate their controller. Real numbers differ by machine, so measure with your workload. The *ordering* of the options is what the model teaches.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Where candidate boxes come from: proposals, anchors and grids
md: Anchors and grid cells are not predictions. They are fixed reference positions that predictions are expressed relative to. A detector with 20000 anchors does not find 20000 objects; almost all of them are scored as background.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: S3 is not just a slow disk. A disk charges nothing per write and lets you overwrite 4 KiB in place. S3 charges per request, writes whole immutable objects, and takes tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds per request. Every design in this course reshapes writes into **few, large, immutable objects**.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Counts aggregate; quantiles do not. If you want to compute a percentile across instances, regions or time windows later, you must store counts per bucket now. That single decision is why histograms beat summaries almost everywhere.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
md: Dense text detectors predict a per-pixel map. EAST regresses a box from every text pixel and merges them; DBNet segments shrunk text kernels with a learned threshold, then expands them back.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access
md: "We check permissions in the web UI" is not complete mediation. If the API behind the UI, a batch job or a debug endpoint reaches the same data without the check, the monitor is bypassed. Ask of every design: is there any path to the object that skips the checker?

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Virtual machines, containers, gVisor and Firecracker
md: Containers share the host kernel; their strength is the strength of that kernel plus the filters in front of it. VMs give each workload its own kernel and put a small VMM on the boundary. gVisor puts a memory-safe kernel of its own in between. Choose by how untrusted the code is: your own services, other teams' code, or strangers' code.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
md: Run operator searches against your own organisation or a client who has authorised it. Downloading files a search reveals, such as a password list, can itself be unauthorised access or handling of stolen data. Record that the result exists and report it.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Chronolocation: telling the time from shadows
md: Shadow length gives the sun's elevation, shadow direction gives its azimuth, and an astronomical calculation turns both into a time window for a known place and date.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: Rebuild cost is decided by the include graph. Touching a header recompiles every translation unit that reaches it, directly or transitively. That is why big projects keep widely included headers small and stable.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
md: A red X on one matrix cell with grey cancelled cells next to it does not mean the other platforms passed. With fail-fast they never finished. Look at which job failed first; that is the one with the real log.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Never reply in anger. Google's guide calls it a serious breach of etiquette that lives forever in the review tool. If a comment stings, ask what constructive point the reviewer is making, and answer that point once you are calm.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Issue first: when to ask, how to report, how to claim work
md: Closing keywords (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`) only work when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**. Aimed at a release or feature branch, the keyword is ignored and the issue stays open after merge.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebasing replays your commits on a new base. Every replayed commit gets a new hash because its parent changed, even if its diff is identical.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: A license is permission plus conditions. The conditions only apply when you do the thing they attach to, which for most licenses means distributing the code.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: A performance claim is an experiment. The PR must let a reviewer rerun it (exact commands, setup, commits) and weigh it (spread, significance and costs), not just read a headline number.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
md: GitHub's "find references" is name-based: the docs say it searches all definitions and references across a repository "to find entities with a given name". Two unrelated functions with the same name in different modules will both show up. Check the file and its imports before you trust a reference.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
md: Automated reduction needs only a yes or no oracle, a check that gives the verdict: does this candidate still show the exact failure? Write that test carefully and the tool does the tedious part.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: Each PR (and each commit in a series) should be justifiable on its own and leave the project building and passing tests. If one depends on another, say so in the description.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
md: A physical block may back many logical blocks. Reference counts say when it can be freed; copy-on-write makes writes into shared blocks safe, at the cost of copying one block.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: what your DNS tells the world
md: Recon results drive scope questions, not actions. Finding that `vpn.example.com` exists does not make it in scope. Check the address against the scope guard before any active step.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
md: In `perf report`, a high Children value does not mean the function is doing the work. main is 100% in every program. Sort by Self to find what executes, by Children to find which caller to change.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Visibility and durability are different events. A store becomes visible when it reaches the coherent cache, and durable only when its line reaches the persistence domain. On ADR platforms, software must close that gap explicitly.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: SPF: which servers may send for a domain
md: Misconception: "SPF pass means the sender is who they claim". SPF pass means only that the connecting IP is allowed to send for the **envelope** domain. That domain may be the attacker's own.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Which end of a storage unit bit-fields start from, whether they may straddle units, and the signedness of a plain `int` bit-field are all implementation-defined in C (cppreference lists them). Two compilers or two ABIs can lay out the same bit-field struct differently, so never use bit-fields to match a wire format or a hardware register; use shifts and masks on a fixed-width integer instead.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A pose model's output is a fixed, ordered list of keypoints per person, each with a position and a confidence. Everything downstream (metrics, angles, rep counting) is arithmetic on that list.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Lattices from zero: points, bases and hard problems
md: The lattice trapdoor in one sentence: the **public key** is a pile of noisy equations, the **private key** is the secret that turns the noise back into something small, and encryption hides a message under more noise that only the key holder can strip away (next lesson, by hand).

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
md: Pre-filtering with a flat scan is exact and its cost is proportional to the number of matches, $sn$. That makes it the best plan for restrictive filters and the worst plan for broad ones.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
md: Do not sprinkle streaming stores everywhere. Intel recommends them for memset-style fills larger than about half the last-level cache when the data is not read soon after. On Skylake server it warns that overusing them on smaller blocks evicts lines you need and can hit a per-core limit on non-temporal write bandwidth.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
md: k-anonymity is a property of one table against one declared set of quasi-identifiers. It says nothing about columns you forgot, other releases, or what the sensitive values in a class reveal.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
md: "We use differential privacy" is not a guarantee until you know three things: epsilon (and delta), the unit of privacy, and who sees the raw data. A large epsilon at event level with a trusted curator can protect very little.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them
md: Diffie-Hellman PSI works because blinded exponentiation commutes: H(x)^(ab) = H(x)^(ba). Each side blinds with a secret it never reveals, so only matching items line up. Hashing alone is not PSI, because hashes of small identifier spaces can be inverted.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 1: reading sudo rules like an auditor
md: Misconception: "NOPASSWD is the dangerous part." It does remove a hurdle for an intruder who has a shell but not the password (a web shell, a stolen SSH key). But a rule that leads to a shell is a root grant with or without a password prompt. Fix what the command can do first, then decide on the password.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
md: A PRM is a per-step classifier read off in one forward pass. Training labels stop at the first error. To compare solutions you reduce step scores to one number; product and minimum perform similarly, but product quietly favours shorter solutions.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Generative PRMs: verifiers that reason before they judge
md: Generative PRMs phrase verification as text generation: write a step-by-step critique, then read the verdicts and a Yes probability off it. They need far fewer labels and lead on error location, at the price of many more tokens per verification and overconfident scores.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: Misconception: "more threads means more parallelism." Parallelism is capped by the number of cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only take turns: they add involuntary switches, push answers later, and make threads evict each other's cache. Extra threads help only when they spend time blocked, as in the I/O scene.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
md: A script is the steps you would do by hand, written down once so they run the same way on every line. Its biggest risk is not crashing; it is quietly counting the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: Hash files in binary chunks, normalize every indicator to lowercase before comparing, and remember that a match means "known bad" while a miss means only "not this exact file".

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Binary quantization = sign of each coordinate, compared with XOR and popcount. It buys 32x memory and very cheap comparisons, but the distance it produces is coarse and has no error guarantee.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
md: v2 is right for requests that arrive one at a time, and still wrong when two refunds arrive at the same instant: both can read "120 left to refund" before either is recorded, and both pay out 100. Every check of the form "read a total, decide, write" is also a race condition. Lessons 5 to 9 make it atomic.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
md: Put the check inside the write, or lock before you read, or let a constraint say no. Then make the database refuse the bad end state too (CHECK, UNIQUE), so a race you missed fails loudly instead of paying out.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to logic and race abuse
md: Log every value-changing event with business context, alert on impossible patterns (one-time actions that succeed twice, bursts within milliseconds, flows faster than a human), and reconcile balances against ledgers. Then contain before you investigate, and retest fixes in parallel.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
md: Small chunks lose their context. D1.5 reads *or adoption. Send leave requests to the People team, who approve them.* It never says which leave. In a real handbook with ten leave policies it would match every leave question equally well. Bigger chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and spend more of the prompt.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
md: Features used for training must be produced by the same code, against the same index state and at the same moment as the features used for serving. Log the vector at query time; do not reconstruct it later.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Trust among thieves: exit scams, takedowns and a fragmented market
md: "The group promised to delete the data" is not evidence. LockBit kept data of victims who paid (found in Operation Cronos), BlackCat cheated its own affiliate, and leaked chats from other groups named victims who had paid for silence. Plan as if stolen data will eventually be published.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The ransom decision: negotiation, proof of life and sanctions
md: A passed proof-of-life test proves only that the actor can decrypt the files tested. Test every size class you need, especially the largest databases and virtual disks, and price the decryptor against what your surviving backups can already restore.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: In practice: register big pools on huge pages, keep the number of connected QPs bounded (share, or use UD for fan-out), batch posts behind one doorbell, inline small payloads, signal selectively, avoid hot atomics, and handle error completions by resetting or recreating the connection.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (mean absolute error, the average size of the gap between predicted and true rating) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: Misconception: reward hacking means the RL algorithm is buggy. DeepMind's analysis points the other way: the behavior comes from misspecification, and a *better* optimizer is more likely to find an intricate loophole that a weaker one would miss. Stronger RL makes the specification matter more, not less.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
md: This grader still runs the agent's code as the same operating-system user, so that code could reach the grader's own files or leave a process running after its own ends. Production graders run the solution in a separate container or user account with no write access to the grader, keep hidden tests, and still watch transcripts (lesson 9). Isolation raises the cost of a hack; it does not prove there is none.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Putting money on risk: ALE and the FAIR model
md: ALE = SLE x ARO is the right *shape* of answer: frequency times magnitude, in money, per year. FAIR keeps that shape but estimates each factor as a range and keeps the full distribution, so you can talk about bad years, not only average ones.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
md: Check the **scope** on any certificate a vendor shows you. A certificate covering "the corporate office in Lisbon" says nothing about the SaaS product you are buying. Ask for the certificate and the SoA, or at least the scope statement, and check the issuing body is accredited.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
md: The engineering lesson from SolarWinds is about **public security statements**: trust pages, questionnaire answers, marketing claims. Every sentence like "we enforce least privilege everywhere" is a claim someone may later test against your internal tickets. Write them so they are true, keep evidence that they are, and update them when the facts change.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Accountability: what boards, CISOs and engineers have answered for
md: Breaches are survivable; cover-ups are not. Regulators judge governance: risk assessed before big changes, audit that reports independently, boards that hold management accountable, statements that match reality, and incidents disclosed on time to the people with authority to decide.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
md: Asynchrony converts idle GPU time into staleness. Every async system pairs a staleness bound (versions tracked per trajectory) with an objective that knows which policy sampled each token: an importance weight from behavior to proximal policy, and a trust region around a recent policy.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: "The root cause" is usually a decision about where to stop asking, not a fact. The SRE book is careful here: systems are complex, and it is likely that multiple factors, each individually not the cause, are jointly causes. Its template says Root Causes, plural. Note that a cause chain pointing at a person is a sign you stopped one question early.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: RRF trades information for robustness: it ignores how far apart scores are, so it cannot be fooled by scale, but it also cannot use a confident gap. With labels and comparable scores, a tuned convex combination usually wins; without them, RRF is the safe default.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Intrusive lists, work items and condition variables
md: Misconception: "`wait` returns only after `notify`, so an `if` is enough." The CondVar docs say a wait may also wake spuriously, and with `notify_all` another waiter may have consumed the result first. Re-check the condition in a `while` loop every time `wait` returns.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy
md: If you hold a task anywhere other than a terminal DSQ, implement `ops.dequeue()` and drop your reference there. The kernel will re-enqueue the task after any property change, so a stale entry means a task is queued twice.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: How secret scanners find keys: patterns, entropy, verification
md: A scanner finds only what looks like a secret. A custom token with no prefix, a password of ordinary words, or a key split across two lines passes silently. If you issue tokens yourself, copy GitHub's design: a unique prefix and a checksum make your secrets findable by every scanner and cheap to validate.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
md: Review the flow, not the line: find each source, follow it to each sink, and check the control (validation, encoding, authorization) at each step. Then ask what the code assumes and whether an attacker can make that assumption false.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
md: A backtracking regex is safe only if every string has few ways to match it. Nested quantifiers and adjacent .* make the number of ways explode, so a short input can take seconds. Rewrite, bound the input, or use a linear-time engine.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: FFI boundaries, release-mode overflow and panics
md: Rust review checklist beyond unsafe: arithmetic on input uses checked_* or try_from, not + or as; every FFI call has a SAFETY comment covering NUL termination, pointer lifetime, ownership and lengths; and no unwrap, expect or unchecked index on anything an attacker controls.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec traps: weak PSKs, aggressive mode, NULL and old algorithms
md: IKEv2 does not make a weak PSK safe. A client that connects to a rogue gateway (for example on hostile Wi-Fi with a spoofed address) completes IKE_SA_INIT with the rogue and sends its own AUTH to it. RFC 7296 states that dictionary attacks on user-chosen PSKs "are not prevented in this authentication method". Strong random PSKs, or certificates, are the fix.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Bell-LaPadula: no read up, no write down
md: Bell-LaPadula protects secrecy only. Writing up is allowed, so a low-level process may overwrite a TOP SECRET file it cannot read. Nothing in the model protects the integrity of data; that needs a different model, next lesson.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The trust algorithm: criteria, scores and context
md: A score hides which factor failed. If a control must always hold (a patched OS for admin consoles, phishing-resistant MFA for payroll), make it a criterion, not a weight that other good signals can outvote.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Idempotent steps: designing work that is safe to run twice
md: Derive the key from the event, let the database or the API enforce it atomically, and reuse the same key on every retry. Then duplicates from webhooks, queues and retries all collapse into one effect.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: When not to automate, and a design review checklist
md: Automate what is reversible, small and precisely triggered; cap and approve what attackers can trigger; keep irreversible, wide-impact and judgement-heavy steps with people; and give language models advice to write, never authority to act.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
md: Path of a vulnerability: found, reported, fixed, numbered (CVE via a CNA), published with a patch, enriched by NVD (CVSS, CWE, products), patched by users. Attackers can enter at any point; the gap between patch release and patch install is where most damage happens.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who does security work: the job families
md: Five families: offence, defence (SOC, detection, IR), AppSec, cloud security and GRC. They need the same foundations this track teaches: how systems work, how attacks work, and how to read, script and explain.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558, a corrected blog and the CSRB report
md: When an earlier statement turns out wrong, correct it publicly, quickly and visibly, and say what changed. Readers make decisions on what you wrote; leaving an error standing keeps those decisions wrong.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
md: Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting. ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Why exact-match caches miss, and how a semantic cache matches meaning
md: A semantic cache trades exactness for hit rate. An exact cache never returns an answer to a different question; a semantic cache does so by design whenever two questions are close enough. The rest of this course is about where "close enough" goes wrong.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Why cloud metadata is the prize: Capital One 2019
md: "It is in a private subnet" does not protect a role's credentials. Temporary credentials from IMDS work from anywhere on the internet unless a policy restricts where they can be used. The attacker used them from their own machine.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
md: Misconception: "SGLang is a prompt DSL, so I must rewrite my app to use it." A DSL, or domain-specific language, is a small language built for one kind of job, here writing LM programs. Most of SGLang's speedups live in the runtime and apply to plain HTTP requests. The DSL is an optional layer on top.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: In practice the straight-line bound is weak on real road networks with travel times: it must divide by the top motorway speed, so it badly underestimates slow city streets. The Bast et al. survey reports the gain is small or nonexistent. **ALT** gets much better bounds from precomputed distances to a few landmarks plus the triangle inequality.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
md: The FFT is not an approximation. It returns the same numbers as the DFT matrix product, up to floating point rounding, by sharing work through $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Misconception: "SVE code is written for a particular width like 512 bits." VLA code must never assume a length; use svcntw() and whilelt. ACLE warns that something like `svptrue_pat_b32(SV_VL16)` loads no data at all on chips narrower than 512 bits.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
md: A pool or arena that never returns memory looks like a leak from the outside. Bonwick's caches give memory back under memory pressure, when the virtual memory system runs short of free pages; your custom pool should have some way to shrink (reset, trim, or a size cap).

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
md: An alert is a question, not an answer. The analyst's job is to answer it with evidence, record the answer so someone else can check it, and feed what was learned back into the rules.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Phishing reports and unusual data egress
md: Volume alone is a weak signal; volume against the host's own baseline, plus the sending process and the destination's owner, is a strong one. Exfiltration to a popular cloud storage service will look normal by destination, so the process and the account doing the upload matter most.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
md: Warnings work when they are rare, specific and opinionated, and fail when they are frequent and neutral. Where the safe answer is always the same, block instead of warning.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
md: Misconception: "it's only dangerous if someone opens a file on the drive". Devices that present themselves as a keyboard can type commands as soon as they are connected, and a network implant needs no user action at all. Controls must act at connection time.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
md: A working SAE pipeline is: cache a site with BOS dropped, shuffle, normalise by one scalar, train with transposed init and unit decoder columns (plus AuxK at scale), then judge it by L0, FVU and delta LM loss from splicing. A released SAE plus Neuronpedia gets you to reading and steering in a few lines.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
md: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
md: Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Long-form and streaming ASR are decoding problems layered on a fixed-window model: the window moves by predicted timestamps, unstable text waits for agreement, and silence must be removed or detected before the decoder invents something to say.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
md: Fast allocators round requests to size classes, serve each class from same-size slabs or spans, and put a lock-free per-thread or per-CPU cache in front. The costs are bounded rounding waste, memory parked in caches, and spans pinned by a few live objects.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
md: Clean file pages are cheap to evict, dirty ones need write-back, and anonymous ones need swap. The kernel approximates LRU with reference bits and active/inactive lists, but once the working set exceeds RAM, even a 0.1 percent miss rate makes memory 100 times slower: thrashing.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Misconception: "out of order is rare, so I can ignore it". In the toy, 5 of 12 readings arrive after a reading with a later event time. Mobile, battery-powered and intermittently connected devices make this the normal case, not an edge case.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: The Transformer's core bet: replace the recurrent chain with attention, so every position can read every other position in one layer and the whole layer runs as parallel matrix multiplications.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
md: A Transformer layer = attention (mix across positions) + FFN (transform each position), each wrapped in a residual connection and LayerNorm, with positional information added once at the input.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: Length normalization is relative to avgdl, so only a document's length compared with the average matters. An average-length document scores the same for every b.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: A GPT is just: embed (token + position), $L$ x [pre-LN causal attention, pre-LN MLP, each added to the residual stream], final LayerNorm, project back to vocabulary scores with the tied embedding matrix.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: A common slip is evaluating the outer derivative at $x$ instead of at the inner value. Here $f'(u) = 2u$ must use $u = 7$, giving 14, not $2 \times 2 = 4$. That is why the forward values are computed and stored first: the backward step needs them.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: A rising loss does not always mean a bug in your gradients. With a correct gradient, too large a learning rate alone makes training diverge, as $\eta = 0.35$ did here. Lowering $\eta$ is the first thing to try.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Do not test your quoting in zsh and assume bash agrees. zsh, the default interactive shell on macOS, does **not** word-split unquoted parameter expansions unless the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is set. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh` (a first line naming the interpreter, the shebang of lesson 4) follow the splitting rules shown here.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: `set -e` is a safety net, not error handling. It misses failures inside functions called from conditions and in `&&` chains. For steps that matter, check explicitly: `if ! cp src dst; then echo 'copy failed' >&2; exit 1; fi`.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
md: Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
md: Bigger batches are not free for users: once the step leaves the flat region (math roof, or growing KV reads), every sequence's inter-token latency rises. A throughput number without a latency number hides this.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Decisions in machine code: flags, compare and conditional jumps
md: Misconception: "the CPU knows whether a value is signed." It does not. `cmp` sets all four flags every time; the signedness lives only in which jump the compiler chose after it.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
md: C is small: a handful of types, operators that work on bits and integers as directly as the CPU does, and `if`, `for`, `while`, `switch` and functions. What makes it hard is not syntax but the rules for memory, which the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
md: `void *` carries an address without a type; the code that receives it must convert it back to the right type. A function pointer carries code. Together they let one function such as qsort work on any data, with the caller supplying the type-specific part.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership answers C's question *who frees this, and when?* statically: the single owner frees it, at the end of the owner's scope. No `free` calls, no collector.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
md: Lifetime annotations do not change how long anything lives. They describe relationships between references so the borrow checker can verify each call site. The function body is checked against the signature, and callers are checked against the signature alone.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
md: $\det A$ is the factor by which $A$ scales areas (negative if it flips orientation). $\det A = 0$ means a direction is squashed flat: no inverse. Otherwise $A^{-1}A = I$ and $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, but in code you call `solve`, and you watch the condition number, not the determinant.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: A loss turns "fit the data" into one number that depends on the parameters. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood for class probabilities. Training means minimizing it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Watch the **gap** between training and test (or validation: a held-out split used for tuning, see lesson 8) error. A small gap with high error means underfitting; a low training error with a large gap means overfitting. Training loss alone cannot tell you which you have.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Suspiciously good validation results are a bug report until proven otherwise. Check that every preprocessing step was fit on training rows only, that no group or time period straddles the split, and that no feature is recorded after the outcome it predicts.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
md: Backprop = for each node in reverse order: upstream gradient times local gradient, summed over every path that leaves the node. One backward sweep yields the gradient for every input at once.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: Locks are for mutual exclusion; condition variables are for waiting until shared state changes. With a CV, always hold the lock, keep the condition in a state variable, and wait in a while loop. A semaphore can play either role, depending on its initial value.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
md: Data journaling writes every data block twice, which halves sequential write bandwidth. That is why metadata (ordered) journaling is the more common choice; OSTEP notes that Windows NTFS and SGI's XFS use forms of it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. The **covariance** $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]$, the mean product of the two deviations from their means, is positive when the two rise together and negative when one is high as the other is low. Lesson 8 develops it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: With little data the prior drives the answer, so state it. A prior that puts zero probability on some value can never recover it: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, and anything times 0 stays 0.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
md: Tokenization fixes what the model can see. Vocabulary size trades sequence length against parameters; the regex and digit rules shape arithmetic; the training data mix decides which languages are cheap; and rare tokens can be under-trained.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Accumulation is exactly equivalent only for layers that treat examples independently. **BatchNorm** computes statistics per micro-batch: with examples (1, 2, 3, 4) in one batch it normalizes the value 2 to -0.45, but in the micro-batch (1, 2) it becomes +1.00. The playbook also notes that accumulation gives no throughput benefit, since it runs the same small batches; it only changes the effective batch size.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
md: Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; lesson 5 shows how libraries handle them.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Reproducible builds: proving a binary came from its source
md: Reproducible builds prove the binary matches *the source you built from*. They say nothing about which source that should be. xz 5.6.1's release tarball contained a malicious build script missing from git; rebuilding the tarball reproduces the backdoor perfectly. Compare release archives against the tagged git tree too (Arch Linux switched xz to building from git when the backdoor was disclosed).

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
md: A closed loop collapses at a rate set by the sample size, and you can measure that rate. A small but steady stream of real data turns the downward drift into a stable level.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: The kernel's view of your memory is a list of VMAs. `execve` and ld.so create the first ones, `mmap` adds, `munmap` removes and splits, `mprotect` splits by permission, and `mremap` resizes or moves. `/proc/PID/maps` is that list, and it is the first thing to read when a mapping misbehaves.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. The formula is the N p at most 0.01 rule from the prediction, solved for p: each leaf may be slow at most 1/(100N) of the time. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Derived numbers go stale. *Years of experience* computed at index time is wrong a month later for everyone with a current role. Store intervals with open ends and compute tenure at query time against the query's reference date, or recompute on a schedule and record the as-of date.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: A TTT layer is an RNN whose hidden state is a model. Update rule = train on the current token. Output rule = predict with the updated model. Choosing the model, the loss and the optimizer chooses the layer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
md: The successors keep the frame (a memory trained on a key-value loss as the sequence streams) and change what it fits and how well. A window or an exact solve protects earlier writes; a robust loss protects against outliers; forgetting decides how fast a changed fact wins. None of it is settled at scale.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: PEAK and TaHiTI: from backlog to handover
md: Both frameworks end the same way: a hunt is finished when its results are documented and handed to the teams that act on them. The query is not the deliverable. The deliverables are an escalation (if needed), detections, data and security recommendations, and knowledge for the next hunt.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The intelligence cycle and intelligence requirements
md: The most common failure is a collection-driven programme: buy feeds, read everything, publish a weekly "threat landscape" digest that supports no decision. FIRST warns that a meeting with leadership that is "informational only" will not go well. Start from requirements and work backwards.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Analytic tradecraft: bias and competing hypotheses
md: Weigh evidence by how well it *discriminates* between hypotheses, not by how much of it agrees with your favourite. Look for the item that would disprove each hypothesis, check its sensitivity, and always keep "someone wants us to think this" on the list.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
md: The numbers are estimates and the tree is never complete. Schneier calls the safe example incomplete and warns not to read its values as a statement about how secure a real safe is. Use trees to compare options and find the cheapest path, not to claim an attack costs exactly 2,200.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
md: Tiers are not the same as NUMA distance. A remote-socket DRAM node is far, but it has CPUs and DRAM-class performance, so it sits in the top tier and is never a demotion target for the other socket. Only slower memory types form lower tiers.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
md: Misconception: a bigger or newer model will beat simple methods. On the M4 data pure ML lost to simple combinations, and on our toy series SES with a fitted alpha was no better than naive. Any model, from Prophet to a foundation model, has to beat seasonal naive under rolling-origin evaluation before it ships.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Revocation: CRL, OCSP, stapling, and why short-lived certs won
md: "We revoked the certificate, so we are safe" is wishful thinking. Revocation reaches clients slowly and unreliably. Assume a compromised certificate is usable until it expires, and size your lifetimes accordingly.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Autotuning has costs you do not see in steady state: the first call for each new `key` value compiles and benchmarks every config, and each distinct constexpr combination is a separate compiled kernel. Keep `key` to arguments that really change the best config, and use `prune_configs_by` to drop hopeless candidates.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: No axis is free. Discrete plus causal is the simplest to train and serve; continuous plus bidirectional plus separate encoders has led the reported GenEval numbers in these papers, at the cost of more moving parts. Pick based on what the product must do well, then evaluate both sides of the model.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
md: Do not assume every unikernel does this. Sealing and compile-time randomization are Mirage's design; a 2019 study by the security firm NCC Group of two other unikernels, Rumprun and IncludeOS, found ASLR, W xor X and stack canaries (a random value placed before a function's return address and checked on return, so a buffer overflow is caught) absent or broken.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: In graph search the expensive part per hop is often the first touch of a random vector, not the arithmetic. Contiguous fixed-size blocks, aligned vectors, prefetching and smaller (compressed) vectors all attack that same miss.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call
md: Read the source, not just the prose. The reward-function doc says the GSM8K scorer (GSM8K, Grade School Math 8K, is OpenAI's set of about 8,500 grade-school math word problems with numeric answers) gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0. A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: World models, and why Genie learns one from unlabelled video
md: A learned world model is not the real environment. Ha and Schmidhuber found their agent discovered an *adversarial policy* that exploited flaws in M, doing well in the dream but not in reality. They raised a sampling temperature, a knob that scales how random M's samples are (higher means more random), to make the dream noisier and harder to exploit. Every world model in this course shares this risk.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: A new head and a higher resolution
md: Preprocessing must match the checkpoint. `google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k` normalizes with mean 0.5 and std 0.5 per channel, while many timm ImageNet models use mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406). Load the checkpoint's own settings (`AutoImageProcessor` in Transformers, `resolve_data_config` in timm) instead of copying numbers from another model.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
md: Temporal ensembling is not a universal upgrade. The pi0 authors tried it early and found it hurt performance, so pi0 executes chunks open-loop: 16 actions then replan on 20 Hz robots (every 0.8 s), 25 actions on 50 Hz robots (every 0.5 s).

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
md: Older guides set the `VLLM_ATTENTION_BACKEND` environment variable. It existed in `vllm/envs.py` up to the v0.14 release and is gone from main. Use `--attention-backend` or `--attention-config` (`-ac`). `AttentionConfig.backend_per_kind` can also set a backend per KV cache group kind, for example a different one for sliding-window MLA layers.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Tiling only helps up to the largest grid the model was trained with. Beyond that the image is downscaled again, and text that was 10 px tall becomes 5 px tall. Check the preprocessing config of the model you deploy, not just the paper.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: Compare&swap is **universal**: an object with consensus number at least $n$ can implement any object wait-free for $n$ processes (next lesson). Fetch&add, swap and test&set are not, so Herlihy proves you cannot build a wait-free compare&swap out of them plus registers for three or more processes.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
md: Blurry long-range output from an MSE-trained model is not a bug in the network. It is exactly what MSE asks for under uncertainty. Lesson 5 shows how ensembles and CRPS avoid it.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Recon at bounty scale: wildcards, subdomains and live hosts
md: Recon results are candidates, not permission. A name found in a CT log, a JavaScript file or a scanner's output is tested only if the policy's scope covers it, and never if the policy excludes it.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Reading a programme policy: scope, rules and safe harbour
md: Scope, rules and safe harbour are read together: an in-scope asset tested with a banned method, or with someone else's account, is outside the protection. Safe harbour never extends to third parties the programme does not control.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefixes
md: HttpOnly is often oversold. It stops cookie **theft** by script, so an attacker cannot carry the session to their own machine. It does not stop script running in your page from **using** the session right there, which is what the Samy worm did. XSS still needs to be prevented at its source.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: PowerShell: objects in a pipeline, and why attackers like it
md: Misconception: "execution policy stops malicious PowerShell". It does not. Treat it as a seat belt for honest users, and rely on logging, AMSI and application control for security.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WEP: how a 24-bit IV broke Wi-Fi's first encryption
md: A longer WEP key does not help. SP 800-97: the technique "has known flaws that are not mitigated by longer keys". The problems are the tiny IV, the linear checksum and RC4's key schedule, none of which depend on key length. If a device only supports WEP, treat its traffic as unencrypted and isolate it.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Android: UID sandbox, SELinux, verified boot and Play Protect
md: Rooting a phone (gaining root, Unix's all-powerful user) or unlocking its bootloader deliberately removes layers described here: verified boot no longer vouches for the system, and root can override the UID sandbox. Fine for a lab device, a serious risk on one that holds work data; device management and attestation checks such as the Play Integrity API (lesson 16) let organisations detect it.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
md: Tokio's local queue is FIFO, not LIFO: the owner pops from the same end thieves steal from. For servers made of many independent tasks, fairness (no task waits forever behind newer ones) matters more than depth-first order. Locality comes from the LIFO slot instead, which Tokio uses at most 3 times in a row to prevent two tasks from starving the queue by waking each other.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy means removing the **CPU copies between the page cache, user memory and socket buffers**. Device DMA still happens. The win scales with bytes moved, so it matters when a program mostly shovels data it does not inspect.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time
md: In a zero-shot classifier, the label text plays the role of the trained weights. Changing a label's wording changes the classifier, so wording, templates, and descriptions are design decisions you test, not decoration.
